case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Arbitration Act’s §1 exemption for “contracts of employment” of “workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” covers workers (like bakery distribution/delivery drivers) based on their employer’s broader involvement in interstate commerce, or only covers workers whose own job duties place them in the stream of interstate transportation.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. § 1 (the “transportation worker” exemption from the FAA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the §1 exemption should apply because they are distribution workers moving goods that travel in interstate commerce, and the exemption should not be narrowly limited to workers employed by traditional transportation companies or only those who personally cross state lines. In their view, when workers are part of an interstate supply chain moving goods to market (even if the final deliveries are intrastate), they are “workers engaged in…interstate commerce,” so the FAA should not compel arbitration of their claims.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue §1 is a narrow carveout aimed at a distinct class of transportation workers—those whose occupation is interstate transportation of goods or people—so it does not reach local bakery distributors whose work is primarily intrastate and not itself interstate transportation. They emphasize that the exemption cannot be triggered merely because the employer operates in interstate commerce or because the products once moved across state lines; rather, the worker’s own duties must involve interstate transportation (or be so closely tied to it as to be part of that transportation function).
key_precedents: Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams (2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that Saxon rejects a crude state-line rule and that some intrastate drivers can be engaged in interstate commerce when they perform a leg of an ongoing interstate carriage. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, a “continuous flow/last leg” test risks shifting §1 from a worker-duty inquiry to a goods-tracing inquiry that is hard to administer and would threaten to swallow the FAA for broad categories of local delivery work—precisely the overbreadth Circuit City warned against under ejusdem generis tied to seamen and railroad employees. New Prime’s original-meaning approach reinforces, rather than loosens, that constraint: it fixes the interpretive frame in 1925 and does not expand who qualifies as “engaged in … interstate commerce” beyond transportation-worker classes. On this record, absent clear evidence that these drivers’ duties are part of interstate carriage rather than local distribution after goods have come to rest, the narrower, duty-centered holding favors enforcement of the arbitration agreements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “last leg of an ongoing interstate journey” theory is the strongest counter, but it shifts §1 from a textual, worker-occupation inquiry into a goods-tracing inquiry that Congress did not adopt in 1925. As the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain, Circuit City’s ejusdem generis reading—anchored by “seamen” and “railroad employees”—confines the residual clause to classes of transportation workers whose own duties are interstate carriage in the relevant sense, not local delivery after goods have come to rest for in-state distribution. Saxon reinforces that we ask what this class of workers does, and on this record that work is intrastate distribution rather than interstate transportation; New Prime’s original-meaning approach does not expand “engaged in … commerce” beyond that narrow, textually grounded category. I therefore see no legal basis to extend §1 here without effectively converting the exemption into a broad supply-chain carveout that contradicts the statute’s structure and our precedents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that these drivers may perform the “last leg” of an interstate journey, but that supply-chain framing dilutes §1’s text and Circuit City’s ejusdem generis limit by converting virtually any local delivery job into “interstate commerce” work whenever goods previously crossed state lines. Saxon, as the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, makes the inquiry worker- and duty-centered—“what she does”—and that approach fits the statutory examples (“seamen” and “railroad employees”) far better than an amorphous “flow of commerce” test. New Prime’s insistence on 1925 meaning does not help petitioners because it reinforces that the residual clause targets transportation-worker occupations, not retail-adjacent local distribution after goods have come to rest. Given the administrability and line-drawing problems and the risk of the exemption swallowing the FAA, I do not see a legal basis to expand §1 here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is the strongest point for Respondent, and I agree Saxon requires a worker- and duty-centered inquiry; but that inquiry can still capture a class of “last-mile” drivers when their regular duties are transporting goods that remain in a coordinated interstate journey to the customer, rather than making stand-alone local retail runs. Justice Alito’s “come to rest” line sounds bright, yet in modern logistics it can be both under- and over-inclusive: goods may physically pause at a depot while remaining in an uninterrupted, prearranged shipment to final destinations, and §1’s text asks whether the workers are “engaged in … interstate commerce,” not whether they personally cross state lines. Circuit City’s ejusdem generis “narrow” construction limits the exemption to transportation workers, but these drivers are transportation workers by occupation and function; the limiting principle is evidentiary—whether their deliveries are part of an ongoing interstate carriage—rather than a categorical intrastate-route rule. New Prime’s focus on original meaning does not, to my mind, foreclose applying §1 where the workers’ duties are integral to interstate carriage as understood in 1925, and the real-world stakes counsel against reading §1 so narrowly that it forces low-wage transportation labor disputes into compelled arbitration whenever the final leg happens to be in-state.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “last leg of an ongoing interstate journey” argument is the best case for petitioner, but it still risks converting §1 into a goods-tracing inquiry rather than the worker-and-duties inquiry Saxon demands. As the Chief Justice stresses, administrability matters here: a continuous-flow test would force courts to litigate supply-chain details and “come to rest” questions in ways that blur Circuit City’s ejusdem generis limitation tethered to seamen and railroad employees. New Prime, as Justice Gorsuch notes, fixes the temporal lens for meaning in 1925 but does not broaden who counts as “engaged in … commerce” beyond transportation-worker occupations; it therefore doesn’t rescue a supply-chain-based expansion. On this record, without a clearer showing that these drivers’ class is tasked with interstate carriage as such (not local distribution), the FAA’s general rule should control.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “last leg of an ongoing interstate journey” theory is the best case for Petitioner, but it shifts §1 from a worker-occupation inquiry to a goods-tracing inquiry that Circuit City’s ejusdem generis limitation (seamen/railroad employees) does not support. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Saxon directs us to identify the relevant “class of workers” by their duties; intrastate bakery delivery drivers are not, in the ordinary 1925 sense, engaged in interstate transportation as such merely because some inputs once crossed state lines. New Prime fixes the original public meaning of “contracts of employment,” but it does not expand “engaged in … commerce” beyond transportation-worker classes; adopting Sotomayor’s continuous-flow approach would make §1 turn on factbound supply-chain minutiae and risk letting the exemption swallow the FAA. On this record, the better textual and administrable line is that §1 does not apply absent proof that these drivers’ duties themselves constitute an interstate carriage function.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “last leg” intrastate deliveries can still be part of an ongoing interstate movement, but that framing effectively turns §1 into a goods-tracing test rather than the worker-occupation inquiry Circuit City and Saxon require. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Saxon directs us to ask what this class of workers does; bakery drivers making primarily in-state deliveries after goods have entered local distribution are not analogous to “seamen” or “railroad employees” in performing interstate carriage as such. New Prime’s original-meaning approach does not broaden “engaged in … commerce” beyond those transportation-worker categories; it instead counsels fidelity to the 1925 public meaning and the narrow, administrable ejusdem generis limit. The alternative “continuous flow” rule would be difficult to administer and risks letting §1 swallow the FAA’s general enforcement rule, a practical consequence that reinforces the narrower reading under our precedents.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “last leg of an ongoing interstate journey” theory is the most serious challenge, but it effectively shifts §1 from a worker-duty inquiry to a goods-tracing inquiry that is hard to square with the residual clause’s text as narrowed by Circuit City’s ejusdem generis analysis. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Saxon requires us to define the relevant class by what these workers do, and then ask whether that class is actively engaged in the interstate transportation function akin to “seamen” and “railroad employees”; intrastate bakery deliveries after goods have come to rest in local distribution do not fit that analogue on this record. New Prime’s original-meaning focus reinforces that the inquiry is anchored in the statute’s 1925 public meaning, but it does not expand “engaged in … commerce” to everyone connected to an upstream interstate supply chain. Because the “continuous flow” approach would invite factbound logistics disputes and risk swallowing the FAA for broad swaths of local delivery work, I remain with Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “last leg of a continuous interstate journey” framing is the most serious pushback because Saxon rejects a simplistic state-line test and can encompass some intrastate legs when they are functionally part of interstate transportation. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, Circuit City’s ejusdem generis constraint and Saxon’s class-of-workers/duties focus mean §1 cannot turn on tracing a product’s upstream travel; otherwise nearly any local delivery job involving out-of-state goods would become exempt, creating severe administrability and line-drawing problems. New Prime (as Justice Gorsuch notes) fixes the relevant meanings in 1925 but does not shift the inquiry from what the workers do to the employer’s supply-chain logistics; on this record, the drivers’ duties look like local distribution after goods have come to rest rather than participation in interstate carriage. Procedural fairness and predictability favor a duty-based rule that preserves §1 for workers whose occupation is interstate transportation, while leaving room for petitioners to prevail on a stronger record showing coordinated, uninterrupted interstate transit.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “contracts of employment” of a “class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and our cases read that carveout narrowly to preserve the FAA’s general rule favoring enforcement of arbitration agreements. In Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams we limited §1 to transportation workers, and in Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon we made clear the inquiry is worker-focused—“based on what [the worker] does,” not on the employer’s broader participation in interstate commerce. On this record, bakery distribution/delivery drivers who primarily make local, intrastate deliveries are not categorically in the interstate transportation class merely because the goods earlier moved across state lines; their own duties must place them in the stream of interstate transportation (or be directly part of that transportation function). A narrow, duty-centered rule best respects precedent, promotes administrability, and protects the Court’s institutional legitimacy by avoiding an expansive §1 exemption untethered to the statutory text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FAA’s §1 exemption applies to “workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” which, read textually and in light of the enumerated examples (“seamen” and “railroad employees”), targets a class of workers whose own duties are part of the interstate transportation of goods or passengers—not workers merely handling goods that once traveled interstate. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams construes §1 narrowly to transportation workers, and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon confirms the inquiry turns on the worker’s “actual work” and whether it is directly involved in interstate transportation, not on the employer’s broader interstate business. Bakery distribution/delivery drivers performing primarily local, intrastate deliveries are not, on that understanding, “engaged in” interstate commerce within §1 merely because the goods previously moved across state lines. Absent a showing that their job duties place them in the stream of interstate transportation (as opposed to local retail distribution), the FAA compels arbitration and §1 does not exempt their contracts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “contracts of employment” of “workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams the residual clause must be read narrowly under ejusdem generis alongside “seamen” and “railroad employees,” i.e., workers whose occupation is transportation. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon rejects an industrywide or employer-based approach and directs attention to the worker’s own duties—“what she does,” not what the company does—asking whether the class of workers is actually involved in interstate transportation work. Bakery distribution/delivery drivers whose work is primarily local, intrastate delivery are not “engaged in” interstate commerce merely because the goods previously moved across state lines or because the employer participates in an interstate supply chain; otherwise the narrow §1 carveout would expand well beyond the transportation-worker class Congress identified. Practical consequences confirm this reading: adopting petitioners’ supply-chain theory would swallow the FAA for vast numbers of local delivery and retail-adjacent workers, undermining the Act’s strong pro-arbitration rule.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts “contracts of employment” of “workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by the “actual work” performed, not the employer’s industry. Properly framed, bakery distribution/delivery drivers who transport goods as the last leg of an ongoing interstate journey are transportation workers whose duties place them in the stream of interstate commerce, even if their routes are intrastate. Circuit City confirms §1 is a narrow carveout, but Saxon and New Prime require that narrowness to turn on the worker’s transportation function and the commerce they are engaged in, not on whether they cross state lines or work for a traditional carrier. Given the real-world consequences for low-wage delivery workers and the remedial purpose of §1 to keep core transportation labor disputes out of compelled arbitration, I would hold the exemption applies here when the drivers’ deliveries are part of an interstate flow of goods.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “contracts of employment” of a “class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and Circuit City requires a narrow, ejusdem generis reading tethered to the enumerated categories “seamen” and “railroad employees,” not to an employer’s general participation in interstate markets. Under Saxon, we identify the relevant “class of workers” by what the workers actually do, and ask whether their duties are directly involved in interstate transportation; local bakery distribution that begins and ends intrastate is ordinarily too attenuated if it occurs after goods have come to rest. New Prime confirms we apply the 1925 common meaning of “contracts of employment,” but it does not expand the exemption to cover workers whose job duties are not in the stream of interstate transportation. A duty-based rule is also more workable and administrable than an employer-based test that would make §1 hinge on corporate structure and supply-chain breadth, risking the exception swallowing the FAA’s rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “contracts of employment” of a “class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under the plain text—read with ejusdem generis in light of the enumerated “seamen” and “railroad employees”—that residual clause targets transportation workers whose own duties are part of interstate transportation, not any worker employed by a firm that participates in interstate commerce. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams requires a narrow, precise construction of §1, and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to identify the relevant “class of workers” by what the workers do, asking whether their duties have a direct, necessary nexus to moving goods across borders in the stream of interstate transportation. On these premises, local bakery distribution/delivery drivers performing primarily intrastate deliveries are not exempt merely because the goods previously traveled interstate or because the employer operates in interstate markets; at minimum, ambiguity would not justify expanding §1 beyond its original public meaning.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FAA §1’s residual clause must be read narrowly under ejusdem generis, taking its meaning from the enumerated categories “seamen” and “railroad employees,” which points to workers whose own duties are part of the interstate transportation function rather than any employee of a firm participating in interstate commerce. Circuit City requires a “narrow construction” of §1, and Saxon directs courts to identify the relevant “class of workers” by what they do and ask whether those duties are “engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” in the transportation sense. On that framework, local bakery distribution/delivery drivers whose work is primarily intrastate and not itself the movement of goods in interstate transit are outside §1, even if the goods previously traveled across state lines or the employer is broadly involved in interstate commerce. This reading also preserves the FAA’s workability and avoids letting the exemption swallow the Act’s general rule favoring enforcement of arbitration agreements.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “contracts of employment” only for a “class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” a residual phrase that must be read ejusdem generis with the enumerated “seamen” and “railroad employees,” i.e., workers whose own occupations are in the interstate transportation of goods or people. Circuit City requires a “narrow construction” and “precise reading” of §1, rejecting interpretations that would swallow the FAA’s rule favoring arbitration. Saxon directs courts to identify the relevant “class of workers” by their job duties and asks whether that class is “actively engaged” in interstate transportation; local bakery distribution that begins and ends in-state, after goods have come to rest, is not enough merely because the employer participates in an interstate supply chain. New Prime does not expand the exemption beyond transportation workers; it confirms that we apply the statute’s 1925 public meaning to the text, which here focuses on the worker’s transportation function rather than the employer’s broader commerce.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FAA §1 exempts only “contracts of employment” of “seamen,” “railroad employees,” and other classes of workers similarly situated—so, under Circuit City’s ejusdem generis and “narrow construction,” the focus must be on the worker’s occupation and duties, not the employer’s generalized interstate business. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by what the workers actually do and limits the exemption to those “directly involved in transporting goods across state or international borders,” which typically does not include purely intrastate bakery distribution routes simply because the goods earlier traveled interstate. New Prime confirms the exemption turns on the statutory text and the worker’s employment contract, but it does not expand §1 to cover all workers connected to an interstate supply chain. Given the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns, the appropriate line is duty-based: local delivery work is not exempt absent evidence the drivers are performing the interstate transportation function itself.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether workers who deliver goods for a bakery are exempt from the Federal Arbitration Act under § 1’s “transportation worker” exemption when their job involves intrastate deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. § 1 (the exemption for “contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (delivery drivers) argue they fall within the FAA § 1 exemption because they are transportation workers whose work is part of the continuous interstate flow of goods: they transport products that traveled across state lines (or are in the stream of interstate commerce) to their final destinations. They contend the Second Circuit imposed an overly narrow test by requiring that drivers themselves cross state lines or work in an industry whose central purpose is interstate transportation, contrary to the text and Supreme Court precedent emphasizing a functional, work-focused inquiry. As a result, they say the arbitration agreements cannot be enforced under the FAA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (bakery and related entities) argue the § 1 exemption is limited and does not cover local bakery-distribution drivers whose work is essentially intrastate, last-mile delivery for a retail/food business rather than a transportation enterprise. They defend the Second Circuit’s approach as consistent with the statutory context (seamen and railroad employees) and Supreme Court precedent that treats § 1 as aimed at workers in the transportation industry engaged in interstate commerce. On their view, merely handling goods that previously moved interstate is not enough; otherwise the exemption would swallow the FAA for vast swaths of the workforce. Therefore, the arbitration agreements should be enforceable under the FAA (or, at minimum, not categorically barred by § 1).
key_precedents: Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams (2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are right to insist, under Saxon, on a work- and class-focused inquiry and to note that an intrastate leg can still be part of a continuous interstate journey, but that framing does not resolve whether these drivers are “engaged in commerce” in the Circuit City sense—i.e., comparable by ejusdem generis to “seamen” and “railroad employees.” The strongest petitioner point is that continuity is fact-sensitive and warehousing need not automatically break the stream, yet on this record (as Justice Barrett emphasizes) the goods are warehoused, allocated, and routed for local distribution, which plausibly marks the end of the interstate movement before the drivers’ work begins. New Prime affects sequencing—we must decide § 1 first—but it does not expand the residual clause beyond transportation workers engaged in interstate transportation as such, and adopting petitioners’ broader continuity test risks the administrability problem Justice Kavanaugh highlights of turning § 1 into an exemption for vast local delivery work. A narrow affirmance grounded in the record’s characterization of post-warehouse local distribution best preserves precedent and leaves room for different outcomes where through-shipment continuity is clearly established.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s “continuous interstate journey” framing is the most substantial petitioner-side point under Saxon’s work-focused inquiry, and I accept that intrastate legs can sometimes qualify. But Circuit City’s ejusdem generis analysis still requires reading the residual clause in light of “seamen” and “railroad employees,” which targets classes whose ordinary calling is interstate carriage, not local distribution that begins after warehousing, allocation, and routing for local customers. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about employer relabeling is real, yet it cannot justify extending § 1 beyond its original public meaning; the better textual line is whether the class is engaged in commerce in the sense of ongoing interstate transportation, not merely handling goods with an interstate provenance. New Prime affects sequencing (we decide § 1 first) but does not expand the exemption’s substantive scope, so on this record I remain persuaded these drivers look like intrastate retail delivery rather than interstate transportation workers.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that Saxon’s work-focused inquiry can reach intrastate legs when the workers perform an integral part of an ongoing interstate shipment, and I accept that premise. But Circuit City’s ejusdem generis instruction still requires the residual clause to be read in light of “seamen” and “railroad employees,” which points to classes whose ordinary work is interstate carriage in the relevant sense, not local delivery after warehousing, allocation, and routing for in-state customers—a break that plausibly ends the interstate movement. The administrability concern the Chief Justice raises is not mere policy; it reflects the statutory structure and the need to avoid turning § 1 into an exemption for vast categories of local delivery whenever goods have an interstate provenance. New Prime affects sequencing (decide § 1 first), but it does not expand who qualifies, and on this record the drivers look more like local distribution than a class engaged in interstate commerce as § 1 uses that term.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s administrability concern—that a broad “continuous journey” theory could swallow the FAA—is the most serious respondent argument, but Saxon already supplies a workable limiting principle: focus on the class of workers’ ordinary duties and whether those duties are a leg of an intended interstate shipment to its final destination, not merely whether goods once crossed state lines. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett invoke Circuit City’s ejusdem generis point (seamen/railroad employees), and I agree it cabins § 1 to transportation workers, but last-mile drivers who regularly complete through-shipments are still doing transportation work comparable in kind, even if they never cross borders. The warehouse/allocation fact pattern can defeat petitioners case-by-case if it truly breaks continuity, but adopting a categorical “warehousing ends commerce” or “must be directly engaged in interstate transportation as such” rule, as Justice Kavanaugh suggests, risks enabling employers to re-label interstate distribution as local and compel arbitration against low-wage workers. New Prime’s sequencing instruction reinforces that we must apply the exemption where the text and historical understanding reach it at the threshold, rather than narrowing it to avoid fears about the FAA’s scope.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability concern is the strongest respondent point, because a mere “goods once crossed state lines” test would risk collapsing § 1 into a broad carveout. But Saxon supplies the needed textual limiting principle: we look to the class of workers’ typical duties and whether they perform transportation work as part of a continuous, intended interstate journey to the goods’ destination—not to upstream provenance alone. Justice Barrett is right to invoke Circuit City’s ejusdem generis frame to confine § 1 to transportation workers, yet that tool does not justify an atextual categorical rule that warehousing/allocation necessarily ends interstate commerce as a matter of law; that is a fact-sensitive continuity question the respondent can still win on remand without rewriting the statute. New Prime matters primarily for sequencing (threshold § 1 first) and counsels against narrowing the exemption beyond what the text and Saxon’s duty-focused inquiry can bear simply to avoid hard line-drawing.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s administrability concern seriously, but Circuit City’s “narrow construction” and ejusdem generis do their narrowing work by limiting § 1 to transportation workers—not by imposing an atextual rule that warehousing and allocation necessarily terminate “commerce” or that the worker must resemble seamen/railroad employees in employer type or border-crossing. Under Saxon’s work-focused inquiry, the relevant question is whether this class of drivers typically performs a leg of an ongoing interstate journey to the goods’ intended destinations; that rule is text-anchored and avoids sweeping in all local delivery of goods with an interstate provenance. Justice Barrett’s worry that my approach turns on “upstream logistics” is answered by keeping the focus on the class’s ordinary duties and the parties’ shipping design: if the record shows the interstate movement ended at the warehouse (goods held for local sale), respondent wins on facts without rewriting § 1. New Prime reinforces only the sequencing—decide the exemption first—and thus counsels fidelity to the exemption’s terms rather than contraction to ease line-drawing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Saxon rejects an employer-industry test and allows § 1 to reach intrastate legs when the class of workers performs a leg of an ongoing interstate journey. But their “continuous flow” approach still must be tethered to Circuit City’s ejusdem generis limitation—“seamen” and “railroad employees” signal a narrow residual clause aimed at classes directly engaged in interstate transportation as such, not local retail distribution that merely follows interstate shipment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, administrability here is part of faithful statutory construction: if any last-mile delivery of goods that once crossed state lines qualifies, § 1 risks expanding far beyond the comparators and undermining the FAA’s basic scheme. New Prime affects sequencing (decide § 1 first) but does not broaden the exemption’s substantive scope; on this record, warehousing/allocation plausibly ends the interstate journey before these bakery drivers’ local routes begin.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan correctly emphasize Saxon’s work-focused inquiry and that intrastate legs can, in some circumstances, be part of a continuous interstate journey; I accept that framing as a permissible application of the text. But their approach still risks letting upstream logistics (where the goods previously traveled and how the shipper characterizes the chain) substitute for the statutory question Circuit City directs us to ask via ejusdem generis: whether this class of workers is engaged in interstate commerce in a way comparable to “seamen” and “railroad employees,” i.e., an occupation of interstate carriage rather than local distribution after warehousing, allocation, and readiness for local sale. On this record—where the goods are stored and routed for local customers before these drivers begin—the better reading is that the interstate journey has ended, and the drivers’ ordinary duties resemble intrastate retail delivery, not interstate transportation work in the 1925 public meaning of “engaged in commerce.” New Prime’s sequencing requirement is satisfied by deciding § 1 first, but it does not justify expanding the exemption beyond transportation workers engaged in interstate transportation as such, as the Chief Justice’s administrability point underscores.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that an overbroad “continuous journey” theory could, as a practical matter, expand § 1 so far that it undermines the FAA’s basic rule—but Circuit City’s “narrow construction” and ejusdem generis already do the narrowing by confining the exemption to transportation workers, not by imposing an atextual warehouse “stop” rule. Justice Thomas is right that we must read “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” in light of “seamen” and “railroad employees,” yet that comparison still fits workers whose ordinary duties are routine carriage as part of a coordinated distribution chain, even if the leg is intrastate. Under Saxon’s duty-focused test, the administrable question is whether these drivers’ regular work is a direct and necessary leg of an intended interstate shipment to its final destinations; if the warehousing/allocation here genuinely breaks continuity on this record, respondent can win on that factual ground without rewriting § 1. New Prime’s sequencing rule reinforces the need for a clear, work-centered threshold inquiry that employers cannot evade by relabeling interstate distribution as “local.”

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1’s residual exemption for “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” 9 U.S.C. § 1, must be read narrowly and by ejusdem generis with “seamen” and “railroad employees,” who are paradigmatic transportation-industry workers. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams requires a “narrow construction” of § 1, and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon applies a work-focused inquiry that still asks whether the class of workers plays a direct and necessary role in the interstate transportation of goods akin to those enumerated categories. Intrastate bakery-distribution drivers who deliver goods locally after warehousing and inventory allocation are not, on this record, a class of workers “engaged in” interstate commerce in the relevant sense, and extending the exemption to any last-mile delivery of goods that once crossed state lines risks swallowing the FAA contrary to precedent and institutional stability. New Prime Inc. v. Oliveira reinforces attention to statutory text and historical meaning but does not compel extending § 1 beyond transportation workers with a direct connection to interstate carriage.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only "contracts of employment of seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce," and under ejusdem generis that residual clause must be read in light of the enumerated transportation-industry categories. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams held the exemption warrants a narrow, precise construction, confining it to classes of workers akin to seamen and railroad employees rather than any worker who happens to handle goods that once moved interstate. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon further confirms the inquiry is class-of-workers focused, but nothing in the text as originally understood in 1925 suggests that intrastate bakery-distribution drivers—whose work is local delivery for a retail/food enterprise—are “engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” in the same sense as those enumerated transportation workers. Because the drivers’ work is intrastate and not part of a class comparable to seamen or railroad employees, the FAA applies and the arbitration agreements are enforceable.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1’s residual clause covers only those “class[es] of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce” in a way analogous to “seamen” and “railroad employees,” and this Court has required a narrow, textually cabined reading under ejusdem generis. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams instructs that the exemption must be given a “narrow construction” and “precise reading,” and Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon emphasizes focusing on the actual work performed and whether it plays a direct and necessary role in interstate transportation. Bakery drivers making purely intrastate, last-mile deliveries for a non-transportation business, even of goods that previously moved interstate, are not sufficiently “engaged in” interstate commerce within § 1; adopting petitioners’ broader theory would risk swallowing the FAA for large portions of the local delivery workforce. Accordingly, the arbitration agreements are not categorically barred by § 1 and may be enforced under the FAA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the inquiry is functional and work-focused, not dependent on whether the employer is in the transportation “industry” or whether the worker personally crosses state lines. Where drivers’ primary job is delivering goods that are moving in a continuous interstate flow to their final destinations, their intrastate leg can still be part of interstate commerce for purposes of § 1’s transportation-worker exemption. Circuit City confirms § 1 is a narrow carve-out, but it does not justify adding an atextual industry requirement that would deny protection to workers performing interstate-transportation functions. Given the FAA’s remedial limits and the practical impact of compelled arbitration on low-wage delivery workers, § 1 should be applied to cover this class of workers when their deliveries complete interstate shipments.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the “class of workers” is defined by the work actually performed, not the employer’s industry. Here, bakery delivery drivers who move goods as part of a continuous interstate journey to their final customers can qualify as transportation workers “engaged in … interstate commerce” even if their own routes are intrastate, because their function is to carry goods in the interstate flow. Circuit City requires a narrow, ejusdem generis reading tied to the transportation-related nature of “seamen” and “railroad employees,” but Saxon confirms that last-mile workers can still fit when their duties are integral to moving cargo in interstate commerce. Applying that work-focused approach, these drivers’ job—delivering goods that remain in the stream of interstate commerce until final delivery—brings them within § 1’s exemption, so the FAA cannot compel arbitration.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Saxon the inquiry is work-focused: we define the relevant class by what these drivers do and ask whether that work is directly involved in moving goods in interstate commerce. If these bakery drivers regularly perform the last leg of a continuous interstate journey—delivering goods that remain in the stream of commerce to their intended destinations—then they are “engaged in” interstate commerce even if they do not personally cross state lines, consistent with the statute’s text and 1925-era meaning. Circuit City requires a narrow, ejusdem generis reading, but that cabining principle limits the exemption to transportation workers; it does not justify adding an extra-textual “must work for a transportation company” requirement. Any remaining ambiguity about the exemption’s scope should be resolved by adhering to the FAA’s enacted terms rather than expanding its coverage by judicial gloss.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1 of the FAA exempts only “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams that residual clause is read narrowly to cover transportation workers similar in kind to those enumerated categories. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon instructs that courts must define the relevant “class of workers” by the workers’ own duties and asks whether that class is directly involved in transporting goods across state or international borders; intrastate bakery-distribution drivers generally are not, merely because the goods they deliver once traveled interstate. Extending § 1 to local last-mile delivery for a non-transportation business risks swallowing the FAA for large portions of the workforce, an unworkable result inconsistent with the FAA’s structure and our precedent emphasizing a limited exemption. New Prime confirms the exemption’s primacy where it applies, but it does not expand § 1 beyond workers whose work is itself part of interstate transportation as Saxon describes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1 exempts only “seamen, railroad employees, or any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under ejusdem generis that residual clause must be read in light of the enumerated transportation occupations. Circuit City Stores, Inc. v. Adams requires a “narrow construction” and “precise reading” of § 1, which counsels against extending the exemption to local bakery-distribution drivers merely because the goods they deliver previously moved in interstate commerce. Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon directs courts to define the relevant “class of workers” by the work they “typically carry out,” and while those workers may perform an intrastate leg of interstate transportation in some settings, the record here describes last-mile retail/food deliveries not akin to the transportation roles of “seamen” and “railroad employees.” Reading § 1 to cover any intrastate delivery of previously interstate goods would untether the exemption from its textual limits and risk swallowing the FAA’s general enforceability rule.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1 exempts “any other class of workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce,” and under Southwest Airlines Co. v. Saxon the inquiry is functional and centered on what the workers actually do, not on whether they personally cross state lines or whether their employer is formally in the transportation industry. Where these drivers’ regular job is delivering goods that remain in a continuous interstate flow until they reach their final customers, they are “engaged in interstate commerce” within the meaning of § 1, and the FAA cannot be used to compel arbitration. Circuit City’s narrow-construction and ejusdem generis principles still leave room for workers whose duties, like loading/unloading in Saxon, are an integral part of interstate movement of goods, and New Prime confirms courts must resolve the § 1 exemption question before enforcing arbitration under the FAA. Procedural fairness and practical consequences also favor a clear work-focused test that does not allow employers to evade § 1 by labeling interstate distribution work as purely “local” last-mile delivery.
